**ChatGPT connects to US bank accounts, raising consent questions elsewhere**

*OpenAI's move to let ChatGPT access bank data via Plaid tests how AI agents interact with open banking frameworks, with Australia already flagging regulatory friction.*

OpenAI has enabled ChatGPT to connect to users' bank accounts through Plaid's open banking APIs in the US, allowing the AI assistant to view balances, transactions and spending patterns. The feature represents one of the first mainstream uses of an AI agent accessing live financial data through third-party APIs, rather than through a bank's own app or a dedicated personal finance tool.

Australia's financial advice sector is watching closely. Industry figures have noted that the country's Consumer Data Right framework and tighter consent requirements would make a direct equivalent difficult to launch without significant adaptation. The question is not whether AI agents will access banking data — that is a matter of when — but whether existing consent and liability frameworks are built for a world where the party requesting data is an autonomous agent rather than a human user.

For European open banking, the implications are direct. PSD3 and the Financial Data Access regulation are being drafted with human-initiated consent flows in mind. Agentic access — where an AI acts on a user's behalf across multiple data holders — sits awkwardly within those models. How regulators respond to this US precedent will shape whether Europe's frameworks accommodate or constrain the next generation of data-driven financial services.

*Sources: [Domestic sector watches on as ChatGPT allows for banking app linkage](https://www.ifa.com.au/domestic-sector-watches-on-as-chatgpt-allows-for-banking-app-linkage/) — IFA*

**Fintechs use open banking data to detect gambling harm before it escalates**

*A growing body of UK fintech practice is using transaction data accessed via open banking to identify early signs of problem gambling, shifting intervention upstream from the point of crisis.*

UK fintechs are building affordability and vulnerability checks that draw on open banking transaction data to flag patterns of gambling harm. When a consumer gives consent, providers can see gambling spend alongside rent, loan repayments and income, constructing a fuller picture of financial stress than any single institution holds alone.

The approach is significant because it moves the detection point. Traditional responsible gambling tools rely on operator-side data — deposit limits, session length, self-exclusion registers. Open banking enables a cross-institutional view that can surface problems a single operator cannot see, such as a customer spreading losses across multiple platforms while falling behind on essential payments.

This sits alongside recent concerns about offshore casinos exploiting open banking payment rails to circumvent consumer protections. The same infrastructure that enables harm detection can, without adequate safeguards, facilitate the spending that causes harm. The UK's evolving framework — encompassing the FCA's open banking oversight, the Gambling Commission's affordability proposals and the PSR's fraud rules — will need to reconcile these competing dynamics.

*Sources: [FinTech, open banking and early detection of gambling harm](https://businesscloud.co.uk/news/betting-on-the-user-how-fintechs-use-data-to-spot-gambling-harm-before-it-happens/) — BusinessCloud*

**Cato Institute challenges US GUARD Act as misguided open banking regulation**

*The Cato Institute has published a critique of the bipartisan GUARD Financial Data Act, arguing it would impose unnecessary regulatory overhead on open banking arrangements that already function through market-driven agreements.*

The GUARD Financial Data Act, introduced in the US Congress as a bipartisan response to the CFPB's stalled Section 1033 rulemaking, would establish federal standards for third-party access to consumer financial data. The Cato Institute's critique argues the bill reflects a "pro-regulatory consensus" that misreads how open banking already works in practice, where banks and fintechs negotiate secure data-sharing arrangements bilaterally, often specifically to eliminate screen scraping.

The think tank's core objection is that mandating standardised access frameworks could undermine the commercial incentives that have driven banks to open APIs voluntarily. It draws an implicit contrast with the European model, where regulatory mandates under PSD2 preceded widespread API adoption, and where the resulting infrastructure has been criticised for uneven quality precisely because banks lacked commercial motivation to build well.

For European observers, the US debate is instructive. The GUARD Act represents one answer to the question Europe is also confronting under the proposed Financial Data Access regulation: whether data sharing works better when compelled by statute or enabled by market negotiation. The Cato critique, whatever one makes of its libertarian premises, articulates the tension clearly.

*Sources: [The GUARD Financial Data Act Reflects a Misguided Pro-Regulatory Consensus](https://www.cato.org/blog/guard-financial-data-act-reflects-misguided-pro-regulatory-consensus) — Cato Institute*

**BlinkPay and BNZ prove real-time open banking payments in New Zealand**

*New Zealand's BlinkPay has demonstrated real-time account-to-account payments averaging two seconds using existing open banking infrastructure, with BNZ the first bank to participate.*

BlinkPay has completed a proof of concept showing that real-time payments can work in New Zealand using existing open banking rails, without waiting for a dedicated instant payments system. In tests with BNZ, funds appeared in recipient accounts in an average of two seconds, using the bank's existing infrastructure and the Payments NZ API framework.

New Zealand currently lacks a real-time retail payments system comparable to the UK's Faster Payments or Europe's SEPA Instant. The standard interbank settlement cycle runs overnight. BlinkPay's demonstration is significant because it shows open banking payment initiation can deliver a real-time experience within a market where the underlying payment infrastructure does not yet support it natively, by keeping the transaction within a single bank's ledger.

The limitation is obvious: this works for same-bank transfers. Cross-bank real-time settlement still requires infrastructure New Zealand has not yet built. But as a proof point for open banking's potential to accelerate payment experiences ahead of system-level upgrades, it is relevant beyond New Zealand. Markets with slower legacy infrastructure — and there are several in Europe's periphery — face the same question of whether overlay services can bridge the gap.

*Sources: [BlinkPay and BNZ prove real-time payments capability using open banking](https://www.bnz.co.nz/about-us/news/blinkpay-and-bnz-prove-real-time-payments-capability-using-open-banking) — BNZ | [BlinkPay proves 'near instant' payments](https://www.nbr.co.nz/te-ao-maori/blinkpay-proves-near-instant-payments/) — NBR | [In a blink: BlinkPay proofs Kiwi real-time payments](https://businessdesk.co.nz/article/finance/in-a-blink-blinkpay-proofs-kiwi-real-time-payments) — BusinessDesk*
